articles.title: ‘We’re looking at a 30-year run’: UK pair aim to complete world’s most complex board game
articles.summary: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa. “We have had a six-turn practice run. It took about 18 months,” said Andy Taeger, with what seemed like a chuckle as he contemplated playing the world’s most complicated board game.
body: “Based on that, we are looking at a 20- to 30-year run for the full game,” said his gaming partner James Purcell. “We’ve come to terms with it.”
The Guardian joined the pair in a Newcastle front room on Friday as they prepared to start an insane odyssey, playing the legendarily knotty war game The Campaign for North Africa.

If they finish it – and that, subject to the events of the next two to three decades, is the intention – they will become the first people known to have completed a game so vast, detailed and time-consuming that it has achieved mythical status in board gaming communities. It is a holy grail.

Purcell, 29, is a mental health worker from Wallsend, Taeger, 30, a software developer from Gosforth. They’re happy to be called geeks. They met about 10 years ago and realised straight away that they had a connection.
points: Decades from now, friends may become first people known to have finished The Campaign for North Africa.

articles.title: Tim Dowling: having a tortoise reminds you that life is long
articles.summary: My wife got ours when she was eight, and he came to live with us soon after we got married. I don’t remember anything about that in the vows. It is the first truly bleak day of autumn – the sky is a deep grey and a steady drizzle is falling.
body: Except it isn’t, quite, as a few hours later the cloud begins to break up and a shaft of watery sunlight reaches the brick step just outside my office shed. When I open the door to let in the warm afternoon air, I find the tortoise sitting there.

There aren’t many pets that allow you to forget their existence for any length of time. The cat reminds me that I have a cat twice a day. The dog will not let me forget I have a dog for half an hour. But it has been at least a week since it even occurred to me that I have a tortoise.
“All good?” I say. The tortoise winds its neck anticlockwise, so it can fix me with its right eye.

Certain experiences – raising children, say, or stepping into the path of a bus – remind you that life is short. But many other experiences remind you that it’s long – mostly things breaking, and then breaking again. I have measured out my life in dual-function push-button kitchen tap spray head replacements – they last, on average, about three years, and according to my order history, I’m on my fourth one.

articles.title: ‘Apologies for any confusion!’: how to write the perfect passive-aggressive email
articles.summary: In a survey, ‘just to be clear’ came out as the most loathed phrase. But I think I can do better. A new contender for the most passive-aggressive email phrase has emerged.
body: If you ask me, these all verge on actual aggressive. Imagine saying “just to be clear” out loud to another person: that’s a conversational poke in the ribs, isn’t it? It’s the kind of thing you unleash 10 minutes into an ill-tempered wrangle with your home insurance company about inflated renewal premiums. “Kindly note” is even worse – it’s a phrase from an angry message on the office kitchen wall about microwave abuse.

No, we can do better than that, or at least I – a person whose own spouse frequently describes her as unpleasantly passive-aggressive – can. Let me explain: an exchange of professional passive-aggressive emails is a ritual as intricately coded as a Belle Epoque duel and it demands the appearance of great politeness. Your message needs to read, on its surface, as exquisitely helpful and friendly, while leaving every cc and bcc on the thread in no doubt as to it what it really is: an epistolary shanking.

articles.title: Beauty Marks: The Best Beauty Looks of the Week
articles.summary: From sculptural updos and dramatic bangs to frosted lids and full-body glitter, this week’s best beauty looks were anything but understated.
body: Welcome back to Beauty Marks: Vogue ’s weekly edition of the best moments in celebrity beauty, from Vogue editors’ IG feeds, and all the glam of the fashion and pop culture landscapes. Each week, we curate the nail art to pin for your next nail appointment, new recruits to ‘Team Bob’, and major red carpet moments from the week’s most glamorous affairs. As always, it’s as much about celebrity beauty as it is about the makeup artists, hairstylists, and nail artists, as well as the creators crafting the trends you’re about to see everywhere.

This week, beauty was all about making an impression. From Chappell Roan’s fiery Titian-red waves and Lily Allen’s lash-grazing bangs to Amandla Stenberg’s sculptural kiss curl, hair took on a particularly theatrical turn. Elsewhere, Doechii made a case for head-to-toe glitter, Charli XCX doubled down on smoky, indie-sleaze eyes, and Nara Smith brought frosted lids back into focus. Whether borrowing from the beauty archives or pushing things somewhere more experimental, there was plenty to look at.

articles.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island
articles.summary: Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures.
body: Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality.

On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon.

I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing.

articles.title: We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee
articles.summary: A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. These days, Bushwick is perhaps best known for its graffiti art, ecuavolley, and queer bars; the Brooklyn neighborhood is famous for its…
body: Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says.

So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.”

articles.title: ‘A Few Good Men’ Marked Its Broadway Opening With a Few Starry Friends
articles.summary: Before it was an Oscar-nominated drama, “A Few Good Men” premiered on Broadway in 1989, helping to launch the career of its 20-something playwright, Aaron Sorkin. Now, nearly four decades later, the work has returned to the Main Stem, directed by six-time Tony Award winner Michael Arden.
body: The work—a thrilling study of military honor, institutional might, and a dauntless pursuit of the truth—is now brought to life by Tom Blyth, who makes his Broadway debut as Daniel Kaffee, the brash Navy lawyer portrayed by Cruise onscreen. Initially more interested in negotiating a convenient settlement than fighting for justice, Kaffee finds himself drawn into a trial involving two young Marines accused of killing a fellow serviceman after carrying out an illegal order. In so doing, he gets to know the darker side of the Corps.

For Blyth, who broke out on film in The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, the play pushed him into new territory. “I’m excited. My whole career so far has been about testing myself and trying to do things I’ve not done yet,” the Juilliard-trained British actor told Vogue on the red carpet. “To be totally transparent, the first couple of weeks were terrifying, but I’ve learned that if I mess up, I’ve got to keep going. Quite literally, the show must go on. It’s the most invigorating way to act, and it makes you a better screen actor as well. If you can do this, you’re infinitely better on screen.”

articles.title: Angels & Demons: Inside ABT’s Theatrical and Fashion-Filled Fall Gala, Honoring Cynthia Erivo
articles.summary: American Ballet Theatre kicked off Halloweekend a little early on Thursday evening with its Angels & Demons–themed Fall Gala at Lincoln Center, honoring the shapeshifting talents of Grammy, Emmy, and Tony Award–winning actress, musician, and producer Cynthia Erivo
body: During cocktail hour, a fashionable crowd, which included designers Michael Kors and Phillip Lim, spilled onto the theater’s portico to enjoy the unseasonably warm October weather. Red devil horns dotted the crowd, though there was no shortage of heavenly apparitions. Bronx and Banco designer Natalie De’Banco, stylist Elizabeth Sulcer, and Nicky Hilton Rothschild channeled Charlie’s Angels in coordinating white looks, while Tina Leung looked positively celestial in a gold Jason Wu gown. Nearby, author Sarah Hoover, in a Carolina Herrera opera cape, Markarian gown, and Maison Michel halo juxtaposed her friend Charlotte Groeneveld’s sleek black look by Khaite.

Many of the dancers, who had to pull off lightning-fast changes after posing on the step-and-repeat ahead of the performance, took a less literal approach to the good-versus-evil dress code. “I chose black, silver, and gold to represent the theme,” said ABT’s fairy godfather PJ Pascual, the stylist who dressed Christine Shevchenko, Hee Seo, Scout Forsythe, and Lauren Bonfiglio in Monique Lhuillier sequins. Catherine Hurlin also embraced a little sparkle in Akris.

articles.title: Where to Eat, Stay, and Play on Easter Island, the Wild, Remote Island in the Pacific
articles.summary: Also known as Easter Island, this Polynesian isle has long been an aspirational destination—here's how to visit.
body: Today, this Chilean territory is essentially an open-air archaeological museum, with many of its enigmatic moai (representations of Polynesian ancestors) returned to their upright positions following seven decades of restoration. Of course to see Rapa Nui only through its superhuman past is to miss much of the story: The island’s distinct Polynesian culture remains a vital presence, particularly in its sole town, Hanga Roa, where nights come alive with cheerful ukulele music and hip-swirling dances. There’s also a vast, vibrant sea, windswept volcanic plains, and a food culture that draws on the island’s rich heritage and maritime setting.
As a repeat visitor to the island, this is my guide to Rapa Nui.

articles.title: Zara’s New Arrivals Have Fall and Winter Dressing Covered
articles.summary: From Leather Jackets to Party Dresses, Zara’s New Arrivals Have It All
body: If you’ve been waiting for an excuse to refresh your winter wardrobe before the holiday season kicks into high gear, Zara’s latest arrivals offer plenty of them. The Spanish retailer has been particularly busy lately, rolling out everything from party-ready pieces and fashion-forward workwear to cozy staples and new designer collaborations.

One of the key moments this week is the latest iteration of Zara’s partnership with Caramel London, the British label known for its playful prints and slightly nostalgic aesthetic. The new collection is filled with versatile separates, printed dresses, and charming accessories.

There are also still standout pieces available from last week’s fall/winter 2026 Studio release, Zara’s limited-edition line of premium-feeling fabrics and intricate details. This time around, the assortment feels especially suited to the holidays, with lace, jacquard-like textures, and embroidery appearing alongside a rich palette of tobacco, oxblood, and chocolate brown.
